title: From 30 October, employers answer for harassment by clients and delegates unless they took all reasonable steps
seo_title: Employers liable for third-party harassment from 30 October
dek: The sixth commencement regulations under the Employment Rights Act 2025 switch on the sexual harassment and third-party harassment duties on 30 October. The six-month limit for most tribunal claims has applied since 1 October. What both mean for crews who spend their working day among clients and delegates.
summary: From 30 October 2026, employers are liable for third-party harassment unless they took all reasonable steps. Most tribunal claims now get six months.
body:
From 30 October, an employer can be liable when its staff are harassed by a client, a contractor or someone at a conference, unless it took all reasonable steps to prevent it. The [Commencement No. 6 regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/1065/made) under the Employment Rights Act 2025 (SI 2026/1065) were made on 1 October, and regulation 3 switches on sections 20, 21, 22, 56, 59, 60, 64 and 65 of the Act on 30 October.

Three of those matter on a show floor. The regulations list section 20 as "employers to take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment". Section 21 is harassment by third parties. Section 22 is a power to make provision about "reasonable steps".

One change is already live. Since 1 October, the time limit for most Employment Tribunal claims has been six months rather than three, according to the government's [timeline](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-the-plan-to-make-work-pay-and-employment-rights-act/plan-to-make-work-pay-and-employment-rights-act-timeline-update).

## Who counts as a third party

[Acas](https://www.acas.org.uk/employment-rights-act-2025/harassment-law-changes) does not hedge: "On 30 October 2026 the law will change so employers will be liable for harassment from third parties." The next line is the one to pin up in the production office: "This will be unless you have taken all reasonable steps to prevent it." GOV.UK describes the same duty as "an obligation on employers not to permit the harassment of their employees by third parties".

Neither asks you to make a conference harassment-free by force of will. The question is what you did, and what you can show you did, before the doors opened.

Acas's list of third parties reads like a call sheet: clients, "self-employed consultants, contractors or tradespeople" and "people at conferences or events". [Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/10/uk-employment-rights-act-2025-october-reforms-taking-effect), a law firm, goes wider: a third party is "anyone other than an employer or one of its employees". On that definition, the freelancer running graphics beside an AV company's employed crew is a third party to them, and so is the venue's duty manager. A hall full of delegates and a client who has found the free bar is, in our view, about as third-party as a workplace gets.

Morgan Lewis also says the bar for a claim has dropped: under the Act, an employee need only show that third-party harassment took place in the course of their employment and that the employer failed to take all reasonable steps. Under the old law, as the firm describes it, an employer was liable only if an employee had been harassed by a third party on at least two occasions. It adds that compensation may be increased by up to 25% where an employer failed in its preventative duty in a successful sexual harassment claim. That is the firm's figure; we have not read the provision behind it.

## Six months on the clock

The longer limit covers most claims. The exception is breach of employment contract claims in Scotland, where GOV.UK puts the change at 9 November 2026. Morgan Lewis says the new limit applies only where the relevant date (the act or failure complained of) falls on or after 1 October. The firm thinks the longer limit "may also create substantially more uncertainty" for employers.

Our reading, in production terms: a bad night at a November awards dinner could still turn into a claim the following spring, long after the set has gone back to the workshop.

## The union piece

Section 59 covers trade union access to workplaces, brought in "so far as not already in force". [business.gov.uk](https://www.business.gov.uk/campaign/employment-changes/employers/trade-union-reform/) still describes the 30 October start as "subject to parliamentary approval". Two details are worth knowing if you run a small crew company. The Central Arbitration Committee cannot impose an access agreement on an employer with fewer than 21 workers, and employers must respond to access requests within 15 working days.

## What comes after

Further out, GOV.UK has the unfair dismissal qualifying period falling to six months for dismissals from 1 January 2027. April 2027 brings extended blacklisting protections, including a ban on blacklists drafted using AI, and December 2027 the regulation of umbrella companies, which anyone paid through an umbrella will want to watch. GOV.UK adds: "All future dates remain subject to parliamentary processes and may change."

The regulations on reasonable steps have no date on GOV.UK. Morgan Lewis expects them in 2027 or 2028 after consultation, which is a forecast, not a timetable. GOV.UK says they will "complement, not replace" the broader requirement to take all reasonable steps, so waiting for a checklist from Whitehall is not a plan.

## Where that leaves events

This is the part of the Act that reaches furthest into event work. Few jobs put staff among clients, delegates, venue teams and other companies' crews quite as relentlessly as ours.

The freelance position is less clear. The official pages we read talk about employers and their employees or workers; none says where a self-employed freelancer stands under these sections. We would not assume you are covered, and we would not assume you are not. What does change, from 30 October, is that you are part of somebody else's risk. Our guess is that companies booking freelancers start putting conduct terms and a reporting route into booking confirmations, if only to show they thought about it.

The client is always right about the running order. From 30 October, that is where it stops.

confirmed.text: SI 2026/1065, made on 1 October 2026 as the sixth commencement regulations under the Employment Rights Act 2025, brings sections 20, 21, 22, 56, 59, 60, 64 and 65 into force on 30 October 2026, section 59 so far as not already in force.

The regulations list section 20 as employers to take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment, section 21 as harassment by third parties, and section 22 as a power to make provision about "reasonable steps".

The GOV.UK timeline, updated on 22 October 2026, says the time limit for bringing a claim to the Employment Tribunal increased from 3 to 6 months on 1 October 2026, with the change for breach of employment contract claims in Scotland taking place on 9 November 2026.

GOV.UK lists for 30 October 2026 a duty on employers to take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their employees, and an obligation not to permit the harassment of their employees by third parties.
GOV.UK says the later power to make regulations on steps will complement, not replace, the broader requirement to take all reasonable steps.

GOV.UK lists the unfair dismissal qualifying period falling to 6 months for dismissals from 1 January 2027, extended blacklisting protections in April 2027 and regulation of umbrella companies in December 2027, and says all future dates may change.
Acas says that from 30 October 2026 employers will be liable for harassment from third parties unless they have taken all reasonable steps to prevent it.
Acas lists clients, self-employed consultants, contractors or tradespeople, and people at conferences or events among third parties.

Acas suggests reviewing client, customer and supplier contracts, putting up-to-date terms on individual bookings such as hotel rooms, telling customers the consequences of harassing workers and training staff in safety and de-escalation, and says all reasonable steps means doing what is possible with the available resources.

business.gov.uk says the union access right starts on 30 October subject to parliamentary approval, that the CAC cannot impose an access agreement on an employer with fewer than 21 workers, and that employers must respond to requests within 15 working days.

Morgan Lewis, a law firm, says the six-month limit covers most claims and applies only where the act or failure complained of falls on or after 1 October 2026, and defines a third party as anyone other than an employer or one of its employees.

Morgan Lewis says an employee need only show that third-party harassment took place in the course of employment and that the employer failed to take all reasonable steps, where the old law needed two occasions, and that compensation may be increased by up to 25% for a failed preventative duty.

Morgan Lewis says the longer tribunal time limit may create substantially more uncertainty for employers.

impact:
**AV and production companies with employed crew.** The duty is yours from 30 October. Acas's suggested steps map onto event work with little translation:

- Review client, customer and supplier contracts and terms. On a job, that means the client contract, the venue agreement and the terms you send to freelancers and sub-hire companies.
- Make sure individual bookings carry up-to-date terms. Acas's example is hotel room bookings; for an event company, read that as each job confirmation, not a framework agreement signed years ago.
- Tell customers the consequences of harassing workers. A line in the client brief and in the delegate joining instructions costs nothing.
- Train crew in staff safety and de-escalation, before the busy weeks rather than after the incident.

Acas says taking all reasonable steps "means doing what is possible with the available resources". We read that as a bar that moves with the size of the company, not a licence to do nothing.

One clause of our own, not one Acas suggests: the right to withdraw a crew member from a situation where they are being harassed, without that counting as a failure to deliver.

**On the day.** Name someone on site, who is not the client, that crew can go to. Write incidents down the same night: what happened, when, who was told and what was done. If a step was considered and not taken, write down why.

**Freelance crew.** The official pages we read do not say whether these sections protect you as self-employed, so assume nothing either way. We expect conduct terms to start turning up in bookings, because on Morgan Lewis's definition you are a third party to the employed staff you work beside. If something happens to you on a job, write it down that night and tell whoever booked you.

**The tribunal clock.** For most claims about acts on or after 1 October, the window is six months. Keep incident notes, and the emails around them, for at least that long.

**Small companies and union requests.** The CAC cannot impose an access agreement on an employer with fewer than 21 workers. business.gov.uk also gives employers 15 working days to respond to an access request, and it does not say the 21-worker rule changes that. Do not let one sit in the shared inbox during load-out week.
verdict_note: The duty starts on 30 October. Before your first show after that, get harassment terms into the client contract and brief the crew. Name a person on site they can go to, and write down what you did.
